utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Registrar, let's call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, I'm Kapila Waidyaratne, for the Prosecution. My colleague, Mr. Nicholas Koumjian will be taking the witness today. Your Honour may excuse him, he's out talking to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is not out. He is in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Koumjian will introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You forgot Ms. Gustin. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours I'm John Ackerman and I'm here with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I thank you and good morning to you too. Today we have Witness 7.40. I take it that he has not asked for and has therefore not been granted any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What I was explaining to the witness is if we do not finish with him today and I expect we will, Mr. Waidyaratne will be handling his cross-examination on Monday because I'm doing Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I hope the Prosecutor will let me do the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both. Let's bring in Mr. Garibovic. Well it very much depends upon you, Mr. Koumjian. His statement is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour in addition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he is a witness that deserves to be here more than a day. I personally -- is it the first time he's giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This is not a Stakic witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No he's not a Stakic. This is why, but I do have -- no, I don't think it's the first time he's giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No it's not. He has testified about Omarska before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He gave evidence in Omarska? That one I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In addition, Your Honour we provided a letter to the Prosecution saying we do not contest the Mount Vlasic events so I don't think it will be necessary to go into much detail regarding those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, that's up to the Prosecution. As usual I do not or I try not to interfere much. But I'm sure that Mr. Koumjian will take into account what you've just stated, Mr. Ackerman. Namely that you are not contesting as such the occurrence of those events you referred to. Mr. Koumjian, you will soon start your examination-in-chief but first let me ask the witness to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have given evidence in this Tribunal before so you know what the practice is. You are holding in your hand the text of a solemn declaration. That will be your undertaking with this Tribunal, with this Chamber, that in the course of your testimony, you will be saying the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. So I invite you now to enter that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Yes. Good morning to you. And welcome to this Tribunal. You are going to be questioned or asked a series of questions by the Prosecution first and the officer of the Prosecution who will be questioning you is Mr. Koumjian whom I understand you already know. After that, you will be cross-examined by the Defence. I invite you to answer the questions in the simplest of ways, shortest way. Don't go at a tangent just answer the question the whole question and nothing but the question and that will almost guarantee you being able to go back home by tomorrow. Otherwise, you will have to come back or stay here over the weekend in The Hague and continue your testimony on Monday. And I can assure you the weekend is going to be pretty cold. Thank you. Mr. Koumjian. Examined by Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Garibovic. Would you state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I am Emsud Garibovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Garibovic, where and when -- where were you born and what year were you born?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Trnopolje on the 29th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is already in the testimony that you gave in the other case where you said where you were born and about Garibi and whatever. Do you confirm to us that what you testified in the other case is truthful, is the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... crux of what you want out of the witness, Mr. Koumjian and forget about the small details. We can refer to them from the transcript of the previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We haven't offered the transcripts of the previous testimony or discussed it. It's from a different case, Omarska, but I will proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in 1992, can you tell us where you were living?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I was living in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually live in Trnopolje or in a hamlet in the area of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In a hamlet called Garibi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your last name is Garibovic. Were there many other people with the same last name in that hamlet?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A village, a whole village, some 80 houses strong was called after Garibovics who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher if you could move please the ELMO so that I have a line of sight to the witness? Thank you. A little bit further back. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in 1992, I want to take you to the day of the takeover of the municipality of Prijedor by Serbian authorities. Do you recall that morning what your experience was?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Like this: Over the radio and throughout the media the population were being simply called upon to surrender, they were also invited to lay down weapons if they had any. That is what I can tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, where were you working?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I was working for a factory called Javor in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That morning, were you able to go to work?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. On a -- en route to Prijedor at the checkpoint I was turned back, together with a number of other passengers who were taking the same bus. The passengers who were turned back were by and large all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they were turned back, describe what happened. Who turned you back?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: At the checkpoint, near Cirkin Polje, they boarded a bus with weapons and they asked us simply for our IDs to look at them. Those who didn't have them but we simply had to all get off the bus because we were told that we had done what we had to do and there was nothing for us in Prijedor any more so that when we got off the bus, we all went home. Others stayed there to wait for another bus, which was to come from Prijedor. Shortly, and others mostly went back on foot, but by and large, all the Muslims who were on that bus were turned back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they boarded the bus. Were these people in uniforms and if so, can you tell us do you know what type of uniforms they were?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were in uniforms. The uniforms were those of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went back home, I want to talk about that period of time between that day, the day of the takeover, and the attacks that you witnessed on Hambarine, and Kozarac. Did you go back to Garibi after being turned back from work?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I did, yes, and after that, I did not go to work any more. I spent all my time at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were you living with at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I was living -- well I had two brothers and two sisters and my father worked abroad in Germany. My mother died some ten years before the war. So I lived in my father's house, although I'd already built my house but we had not moved house yet, since my wife was the housewife. I mean she was looking after the whole household there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said your wife. Did you have any children and if so, what ages were your children in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I did. I had two sons. The first one was called Sead and the other one was called Mirsad. The elder is 18 now and the younger one is 14. So one was born in 1985 and the other one in 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the few weeks between when you were turned back from work following the takeover and the attacks, can you describe what life was like for the people in Garibi?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Life was very bad. People were afraid. We were simply afraid. People, I mean men and women and children, left their homes at night and went to a nearby village called Sivci. And when day would come, they would come back home and engage in whatever business, whatever chores they had. That is tended to their forms and their livestock and so on and so forth. But there was a great deal of fear. People were not there, would quit their homes at night and come back by day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Garibi a village made up of one particular ethnicity and which ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. They were Muslims, although around them there were Serb houses, there were villages such as Radonjici, Nisevici and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any time were there -- was there a checkpoint set up anywhere around Garibi either by the people of Garibi or those from the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A checkpoint was set up in Trnopolje and it was at a crossing on the way to Petrov Gaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who controlled that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That checkpoint was controlled as I have said before, before the split occurred, everybody was involved in that -- at that checkpoint, Muslims and Croats and Serbs. In Trnopolje, there were members of 17 different ethnic groups and prior to the conflict, they were all manning those checkpoints. However, when things fell apart, only Muslims and others stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at one point the checkpoints were mixed and later, the -- is it correct that the Serbs left the mixed checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go now to the day of the attack on Hambarine. First we don't expect you to have a perfect memory for dates. If you do not remember the exact date, that's fine. But do you remember the day of the attack on Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I do. It was Saturday to Sunday, the night between Saturday and Sunday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you become aware of the attack on Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: One could hear shells falling. I could not see that but one could hear shells falling over that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Garibi is actually on the other side of Prijedor from Hambarine; is that correct? It's quite a distance away?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. It's quite some distance away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After witnessing the attack on Hambarine, do you recall hearing any radio announcements?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, that is Sunday, people are invited again to turn over weapons, if they had any, any weapons from pistols, hunting rifles, all weapons. It was pointed out. All the weapons that people had at home, whether they be licensed pieces or not. They were all invited to turn them over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which people were being invited to turn in their weapons, all the people of Prijedor or who was it directed against? Or towards?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims and others only. I mean the non-Serb population, Croats and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were calls for the Serbian population to turn over their weapons by the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were not invited to turn in their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of time in late 1991 and early 1992, leading up to these events, did you see any evidence or become aware in any way of any arming of the Serbian population in the areas of your neighbours in the areas around where you lived?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that nearby Serb villages, one of them, Nisevici that a helicopter landed there one day and simply that some weapons had been brought, and other places such as Radonjici and Petrov Gaj, I could see their lorries arriving, covered with canvasses and they were arriving there and I presume they were also bringing in weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the Sunday, after you heard the announcements regarding the surrender of weapons, what happened? That Sunday, after the attack on Hambarine, you said you heard demands for surrender of weapons. And then what occurred?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, afternoon, around 1.00, that is when several shells were fired on my village, and simply people from my places started fleeing towards Sivci, some towards Huskici and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where you were, could you see any other areas that were being shelled besides your village?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, no, but in the afternoon, when it was already getting dark, the shells started to fall on all the surrounding places with Muslim populations. This happened in Kozarac, Kozarusa, Mujkanovici, Huskici, Kevljani, so all the surrounding settlements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that Garibi was surrounded by Serbian villages; is that correct? Or Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone in Garibi before or during this attack shooting out, firing their weapons at anyone outside of Garibi?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do with your wife and your small children at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I went to a neighbouring village with my wife and children, the village was called Huskici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have some family at Huskici?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The wife of my brother used to live there before she got married.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you all arrived in Huskici?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That evening was just terrible. All the surrounding settlements were shelled all night, until morning. I stayed in that house and the other citizens also stayed in their homes since there was a stream there, some people crossed the stream and fled, but for the most part, we stayed in the village of Huskici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, in the village of Huskici did you see any Muslims or Muslim forces firing or attacking Serbs or other people?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Huskici and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Huskici that night and the next day, I went to Brdjani with my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you go to Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: We had heard from some people that there will be a kind of surrender, a column would be formed and that it would be possible to go to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you -- what happened when you left for Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Everything looked just terrible. All the houses were devastated by the shelling. There was a lot of dead cattle around. Everything around was destroyed by the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you and your family were travelling towards Brdjani? Did you arrive there?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived at Brdjani, and then later, I came back again because we had heard that it was allegedly possible to go to Prijedor. I returned through Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the shelling go on for? You said it started at about 1.00 on Sunday. When did the shelling stop?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that be Monday morning? You said it started Sunday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what --

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It stopped on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you tried to go to Prijedor through Kozarac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see when you went through Kozarac and what happened?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Kozarac was completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and your family joined a convoy or a large group of people going towards Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in a vehicle? Were you walking? Were you carrying your children? How did you travel?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: We went on foot towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that convoy or that group of people, were they organised by any army or police at any point? Did you see any of the Serbian army or the police?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were standing on the sides as an escort on the way to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the people walking? Were all the families mixed together? And at any time was anything organised by the police or army?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: When we started to turn from Kozarac, on the road that leads to Prijedor, we were all mixed up. All the time, men, women, and children were walking along and they were all mixed together. After a while, the soldiers who were standing on the sides regrouped everybody. They made the men walk on one side and the women and children on the other side so there was a division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were walking towards Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then we were stopped next to the Ziko restaurant or next to the Limenka bus stop which was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at this stop?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: The place where they stopped us, they started immediately to beat certain people. They asked if anybody had a knife or anything like that, they confiscated that. People threw those things away. A lot of soldiers were stationed there. There were tanks, mortars on the sides. I could see all of that. And people there were loaded up into buses. The men were loaded into buses, as well as the women and children, but men were taken to certain buses and women were taken to other buses. In any case, there were buses there and we went into those buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those buses from a particular company? Did you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: They were blue buses that I used to ride on every morning when I went to work. They were the blue Ikarus buses of the Prijedor transport company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's also called AutoTransport Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the bus that you were on take you to?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It took me to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see, among the men, were the men all put on buses indiscriminately or did you see any selection of men for various buses?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some were separated and put on the buses. In any case, there was some kind of grouping made. I couldn't see that right away, only later, since most men went to Omarska and only two or three buses of men at that time arrived at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had mentioned your brother, one of your brothers. You had a brother named -- you had two brothers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your brothers with you when you were travelling on that -- to surrender in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. My brothers were not with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the Trnopolje camp, did you find either of your brothers?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't find any of my brothers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived there, did you see your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only in the morning, because when we arrived we were -- the men, we were locked up in a gym and that's where we spent the whole night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next morning you saw your wife. How long did -- is it correct that you stayed at the Trnopolje camp yourself until the 21st of August, 1992? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were your wife and children at the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't stay that long. They were there for a few days and then after that, all the women, together with the children, went to a nearby village called Sivci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Court has heard quite a bit of evidence, I believe, about the conditions at the Trnopolje camp so I do not think it's necessary for you to go into detail but having been there for quite sometime, can you just briefly describe to the Judges what it was like to be in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The conditions were bad. There were no toilets, there was no water, there was mud all around. There was a lot of rain at the time. There was no food. Simply the conditions were really bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Focusing on the period of time prior to the visit of foreign journalists on, I believe, the 5th of August, can you describe what the food was like up until that time?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't get any food, only if we managed to get some food ourselves, or if we had someone to bring it to us. Since my wife was in Sivci, she managed to bring something for me to eat, and whatever she brought, I would share with the others so it was very little. As far as the Red Cross is concerned, it existed but we weren't getting anything from them. People who had money were able to buy bread and those who did not have any money were not able to do that, only if they were given something to eat by somebody then were they able to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned your brothers. Did you learn where your brothers were while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My brother Ahmet was in Sivci the whole time and then after, when Sivci was cleansed of men, he was taken to Keraterm. My brother Irfan was caught or captured in Benkovac with another group, a group of people who had simply tried to cross over Mount Kozara. They just wanted to go to another territory, to Croatia or somewhere like that, but in this attempt, they were captured and the whole group was transferred to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that your understanding was in the group your brother was in, the men were armed? Irfan's group?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did have some weapons from the Territorial Defence, which had been distributed before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn how your brother was treated at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I found that out from men who had arrived. Actually, the first group of people who had been released from Omarska told me about what happened to people whose last name was Garibovic in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to those people named Garibovic in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: One evening, they asked all the persons with the Garibovic last name to come outside. My brother Irfan came out with that group. They beat them senseless on the way out. And then a car engine was heard to start up and they were driven away somewhere and to this very day, nothing is known about those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people from Garibi that you know were taken away that night and disappeared?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That night, 11 people were taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary to give the names of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Some courts are listing the names of victims so we could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly but I think he also refers to some of these details in his previous testimony and certainly, in his statements to the German FBI.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's correct but they are technically not evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly but I don't -- if we need to know these names we will have them admitted. If not we will go ahead. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to that previous transcript, the preliminary information about his date of birth and his family and all that, this list of names that we are talking about now, we will stipulate to all of that and therefore it becomes an official part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also -- so it's not necessary, sir, Mr. Garibovic, to mention all those names which you've testified to before. In the Trnopolje camp, I think you may have been aware that some of the Serbian authorities say that this was a camp only for people who wanted to come. It was voluntary and that you were free to leave at any time. Did you feel free to leave the Trnopolje camp at any time?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't feel free, and people did not leave the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if there was a machine-gun set up at the camp at one -- in one point in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was there. It was placed at the entrance. And there were several such places throughout the camp where there were camp guards who did have weapons. They were armed. They were guarding us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This machine-gun, was it pointed out, as if protecting the camp or was it pointed in towards the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes it was pointed towards the camp. The weapons that were there, that people carried, was in all kinds of positions. It was pointed towards us, sometimes they carried it with them, sometimes they would leave it. But generally it was pointed towards us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about learning about the people or the guards at Omarska looking for people named Garibovic. When you found that out, how did you feel in the Trnopolje camp? Did that frighten you?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was frightened at the Trnopolje camp, and I simply started to avoid such contacts with other people. I was simply afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Trnopolje camp, did you learn of any killings of people who had been inmates there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I'll object to that, unless he can say who it was he learned it from and who was killed and detail, something more than just base rumour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question isn't that -- whether he had heard anything of the sort but whether he learned of any killings of people who had been inmates there. So let's take it -- I understand your objection but I don't think you are right. But let's be specific. While you were in Trnopolje, were you yourself witness of any killings? Did you see anyone being killed while you were in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not, but people left the camp that I know about and never came back again, throughout the time that I spent at the camp. They simply ended up somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you learned about this while you were still in Trnopolje or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was at the Trnopolje camp. I was there for three months and people were disappearing after a month, a month and a half, two months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, I will leave it at that and leave it in your hands, Mr. Koumjian but please try to be as specific as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Garibovic, were there ever any times that the guards asked Muslims, the inmates, to go bury individuals?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was asked and people would go and bury the persons and then come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to any of these individuals who had to bury persons who had been killed from the Trnopolje camp or surrounding the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I would see people leaving and coming back. The people went down that road. I can give you an example here. For example, when Matrici and other villages were rounded up, that night many people were killed and the next day people, other people, went to bury them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of a family in the Trnopolje camp, and I believe the name is Forici -- Forici?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour it's Forici. We have heard this about six times and I've never contested it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Given that I will go on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, taking you up on this, whenever you can intervene along these lines, the Chamber will appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Garibovic we were talking about your feelings of whether you could leave or not. After you learned about the guards at Omarska looking for Garibovics, did you attempt to get out of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One day, since the Red Cross was distributing -- it's like this. When Keraterm camp was disbanded and some people came, but not all, from Omarska, there was a lot of people, it was overcrowded at Trnopolje, and life conditions, living conditions, were impossible and they saw that. So they allowed people from Prijedor, with a pass, to go to Prijedor, but this pass had to be picked up at the Red Cross. It was issued at the Red Cross by Major Slobodan Kuruzovic. So one day I went to collect this pass, since I had an uncle in Prijedor, and I wanted to leave Trnopolje and go to Prijedor. However, I wasn't allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak personally to Kuruzovic, requesting the pass, the permission to leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I saw in that same period people who had applied for this pass and they did get the pass, but I did not, so then I myself went there and spoke to Kuruzovic and he said to me that I couldn't get such a pass. There was a kind of remark or some kind of intervention, as far as I was concerned, and that I was not allowed to go to Prijedor so I returned to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Kuruzovic tell you who had intervened in your case or explain what he meant by there was some kind of intervention in your case?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. He said that he didn't know anything, that simply there was some kind of intervention and that I could not leave the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned prisoners arriving from Keraterm and Omarska. When you saw them, when you observed their physical condition, can you tell us if there was anything noticeable about them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I authorise you to be specific here and go direct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they look like, the men that came from Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Those people were different from us who were at Trnopolje. Those people looked terrible. They had lost 20 to 30 kilograms. They had beards, they were dirty, they had dysentery. I can say that they looked awful. Some of them were beaten. I could see that when they were taking their clothes off, other people had to help them to do that. Some of them couldn't even walk. They had to be helped by others. It was really terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go now to the -- excuse me, at some point in the camp, did the International Red Cross arrive at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How -- when was that in relation to when you left the camp, the 21st of August? Can you give us an approximate date of when they -- the International Red Cross first started to come to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was sometime after the Keraterm camp was disbanded. I can't remember the exact date but it was at that time. Already at that time a group had arrived to Trnopolje from Omarska but at that time, Omarska was not yet disbanded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the 21st of August, had convoys left the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were several convoys which went towards Travnik. Buses and trailer trucks usually went to Travnik. But there were also two or three -- I can't remember exactly but I can say three convoys by rail that went towards Banja Luka and Zenica. I don't know who else managed to get on those convoys but my wife and children did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when your wife was put on to the train convoy, was able to get on to the train convoy?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It was sometime in mid-June perhaps. I can't remember really. I only know it was June, June or perhaps July. I can't really remember. It was either late June or July. I don't know. All I know is that my wife and children left with a convoy going through Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife describe the kind of train it was? Was it a passenger train with benches for seats or? What did she tell you about the train and the conditions in which she was transported out of the area?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Like this: It wasn't far from the camp so that I could see myself what kind of rolling stock was used and what kind of carriages were that my wife left. Those convoys were made of metal. I'd say those were livestock wagons. And she and others left in those carriages which looked more like those used to transport livestock. I mean they were made of metal and they were all closed, there were no windows, there was just one, a door, which in the middle of which opened but of course the door had to be shut during the transport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she describe the conditions during the transport?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: The conditions were bad. Children, old people, a number of sick among them. They had no water. They had no food. They had no air. It was very hot. The train stopped on a number of occasions but the door wouldn't open. They did not know why that train stopped so that it was very difficult, a very difficult trip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On all of these convoys, prior to the 21st of August, was there any selection of the people that could go? Were young men, for example, allowed to get on to these convoys?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Like this: It was mostly women, children and the elderly. Men were not allowed. Men who looked, men who were of a younger age, they could not leave the Trnopolje camp unless they had some money, unless they had connections, unless they knew somebody. Then perhaps some of them did manage to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the International Red Cross. Prior to the 21st of August, the day you left on the convoy for Vlasic, had the International Red Cross registered you and other men at the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No, not during my stay. Nobody registered. So I didn't either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 21st of August, did a convoy appear at the camp? Or let me back -- ask you another question. How did you first learn about the convoy that you were on, on the 21st of August? What was the first information you received about that?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: All the convoys from Trnopolje, people from the neighbourhood were rounded up the day before and brought to Trnopolje and then could be taken away the next day. So if they brought people from nearby places, they would be brought there in the evening and then the next day, they would be sent on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the 21st of August convoy, was there a particular area that was brought to the camp or, or village?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. For instance, when I left, there were people from the area of Dzonlagici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn about the convoy the morning of the 21st of August or the -- or prior to that?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 21st of August, what time did the convoy begin to form? Did any trucks or buses arrive at the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only four buses came from Prijedor. There were no trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Slobodan Kuruzovic present on that morning?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this convoy similar to the others in that young men were not allowed to board?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I can answer that in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Young men were not allowed to board the convoy the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Like this: They did not allow us, but again, on the other hand, they did not stop us. You understand what I mean? They did to the stand by the buses and turn men back. They stood there and saw us get on but had they been standing by the door, none of us would have been allowed to board. So they didn't prevent us but they didn't allow us. We were simply let on to the buses. That is how I can put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were on the bus that you boarded?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Many, many. I'd say, I'm sure there were more than 100, perhaps even as many as 150 in a bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the four buses that you saw arrive at the camp leave together? And if so, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after we boarded them, we arrived in Kozarac. We left Trnopolje and arrived in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Kozarac, did you see other vehicles that joined your buses?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived in Kozarac, then on the main Prijedor-Banja Luka road, we waited to be joined by a convoy which was allegedly to arrive from Sanski Most or Gomjenica, Sanski Most, I know it was something like that. And I know that we waited there for a while to be joined by this convoy coming from the direction of Prijedor and there was all -- there were also trailers, I mean trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this convoy joined you, were you able to see how many buses and trucks, additional, had joined the four buses that came from the Trnopolje camp on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see that, because I was in the bus, but there were very many people and I can say that they allowed, since they there -- since those four buses were crammed, some people were allowed to get off the buses and get on to trucks or perhaps some other buses. I don't really know how many vehicles there were behind us or what else was there so that some people left the buses because they were overcrowded and moved over to trucks, trailers and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The buses that arrived at the camp, did you recognise the buses and if so, could you tell us what company they came from?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Those buses were blue and they were of Ikarus make, the same kind of buses I used to take to go to work and from work of the AutoTransport Prijedor of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the drivers of the bus, if you were able to notice, regular civilian drivers?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the buses arrived, was there any group of police or army escorting the buses that came with you on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of those convoys that were organised were escorted by the military and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular group that escorted you, can you describe the uniforms? Were they all wearing the same uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: In front, the driver wore the uniform of the former Yugoslav army, so that was that. Those who came in vehicles -- in blue vehicles, they had blue uniforms, patterned uniforms, and those were the police. And one or two who were in the front also wore uniforms of the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say blue patterned uniforms, is that a -- do you mean a camouflage or what kind of pattern do you mean?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I'd say it was something like camouflage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those -- the convoy proceeded through Banja Luka and through Skender Vakuf and made several stops which I don't think we need to go into in detail; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It is. I can say that we did not stop anywhere, and that it all went on like that. There were no problems until we reached Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point -- well is it correct that there were several stops at -- following that; is that correct? Following Skender Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Following Skender Vakuf, we stopped several times. I cannot tell you how many times exactly but I do know that we were stopped several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one stop, did you notice an individual carrying a walkie-talkie?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform was this individual wearing?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: He was also in a Yugoslav People's Army uniform except that he also had a red beret on his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe him?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was about 190 tall. He was rather -- his complexion was dark. He was slim. At that time, he also had some kind of a talky-walky in his hand and he was using it to converse with somebody. And when getting off and passing by him on my way to a brook, I overheard him say something like, "Well, in about half an hour."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say that to you or on the walkie-talkie?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: On walkie-talkie because he was talking with somebody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you reboarded the bus following that stop, did you see that man again?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was in the front of the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say or do at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: He simply said, after -- before -- after the separation, because for a while, we all proceeded together but then the bus was stopped again, and then men of my age, older than I am, and younger, were separated or rather we were ordered to move over to an empty bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point, where men were separated, are you saying it was men of approximately military age, 16 to 50, something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, we could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer? Because the interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, those were men of my age, older than I am, than I was, and younger, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were they children and elderly men or only men that were not either children or elderly?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Children and women and the elderly stayed in the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point where you were separated, was it only your bus or could you see if men were being selected from other buses and trucks on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I could not see anything, because as we got off, we were ordered to keep our heads down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see if any men came on to your bus that hadn't been on the bus before? Or perhaps -- let me withdraw that because my question may assume something that's not true. At the point where men were separated, did you get back on the same bus or did you get on a different bus?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. We got on to another bus which was empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that empty bus, did you see only people that had been on your bus or did you see some other men join you?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: We were ordered to keep our heads down, so all I can say is that the bus was full and that there were many people in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I know it's very difficult and -- but please tell me if you can give any estimate of the number of people that were on your bus? Can you give us any idea, after the men were separated, and were you put back on the new bus, how many men do you think were on that bus?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps around 150 in my bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point on the convoy, were you robbed or did anyone demand goods or money from you or others on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On our way, the man with this red beret he had a small bag. So he passed it around and we were told to put in money or jewellery or whatever we had so some people did and put it in this small sack. I mean whatever they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That man with the red beret you described him but did you notice anything about his mouth?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- no, I don't think. I saw when I passed by him, I cannot be 100 per cent sure but I think -- I think he was missing some teeth or at any rate that his teeth were in bad shape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men who were separated, were they put on only one bus or more than one bus?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. I can't answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the point where military-age men were separated, could you see if there was only one bus that you were being put on, the bus that you were on, or was there a second or third bus?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: All I saw was that bus, which I took.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm coming to a point where it might be not very convenient to break in ten minutes. Do you want me to continue longer on break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will break now, Mr. Koumjian, and we will resume in 25 minutes' time. How do you think you're going?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm going well. I think we'll finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine so. In other words, you are confident that you would finish with the witness in the course of the next part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Would that put you in a position to conclude your cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have a very short cross, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could I bring up one matter since we do have a few minutes, I was instructed to bring up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't think it's a problem. There is a witness BT30 arriving tomorrow and the question is do Your Honours want the witness to testify Monday? The witness would be available to testify Monday if that's necessary but we only have four witnesses for next week. We do not believe it will take all week for those four witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was told or rather we were told by Ms. Korner that you had no witnesses for Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And that's why I was asked to relay this new information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My sense is that if that witness doesn't testify that's the witness we scheduled for Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, for Tuesday, exactly. And 7.3 if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we sit on Monday then we probably can't sit on Tuesday because of the way we've arranged to do the witnesses and so if one of those days has to be off it probably ought to be Monday. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We will sit on Tuesday. We will sit on Tuesday because the moment one starts disrupting the arrangements made, everyone usually tries to make some arrangements the moment that there is an opportunity of some free time. So I can quite understand, Mr. Ackerman, that was the understanding until the day before yesterday so let's leave it at that. Okay? And let's try and finish with this witness today. I thank you. We will resume in 25 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry for the delay. Mr. Koumjian, you may resume. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Garibovic, when we were last speaking you told us that after the point of separation, you were placed on the bus, the very crowded bus, with about 150 men. How far did that bus then drive or how much further before you made a stop in that bus, in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Not long, 10, 15 minutes maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were on the bus at that point, were you allowed to look around or was there an order not to?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: We were ordered to keep our heads down, to look at the ground, and our hands at our -- at the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point, or after being separated and placed on that bus, at that point, did someone come to collect your valuables?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that -- please help me because I'm a little confused. At what point -- I believe we talked about the fact that you were asked to give up money and valuables; is that correct? All the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did testify on this earlier on he said a man with a green beret, a red beret, with a red beret and put everything in a bag, and he had a missing tooth or something. So what else do you want to know from him?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 10 or 15 minutes when the bus stopped, what happened?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: The man in the red beret, who was in the front of the bus, told us, "Now you'll get off the bus. And now you're going to be exchanged, living for the living and dead for the dead."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get off the bus and what happened when you got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Like this, we all got off through the front door, because the rear door wasn't open and behind the bus, we formed a column, standing in two, that is how we were ordered to stand, in a line of two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got off the bus, did everyone from your bus exit and form those two lines? Was it your entire bus that was then lined up outside, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All people got off my bus, but when I got off, I could see some ten metres away that there was another identical bus standing in front of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone get off that bus yourself? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were lined up at that point, can you describe the area that you were in, what it looked like? What was the road like?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: The road was all stones, and across from us where we lined, there was an elevation, but it was rocky, that is a rocky area, and the road, it wasn't asphalt. It looked paved with stones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say there was an elevation on one side, do you mean that there was a sheer rock face on one side of the road?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. As we were lined up in those two lines, this rock was behind us and on the other side, there was a chasm. So in other words it was a wood path, a forest path, which was cut through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you were lined up in the two rows?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: We were ordered to turn to the right, and then the command was to simply start, to move, lined as we were, except that we had to keep our heads down and our hands had to be on our backs. One of the colleagues who was there did not keep his head sufficiently down, I remember this well, and a soldier came up and hit him so badly that he fell straight away, and then told us we had to keep our heads down as much as possible, and hands at the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the order then?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Then we were ordered to turn and proceed, and I can say that we went on foot for some 10 or 15 minutes from the place I mean where we had got off the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were walking in two lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Walking, yes. And then the command was to stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: To step forward two paces. I don't remember whether it was two or three, but be that as it may, we were told to turn towards the chasm and to make two or three steps forward. As I was the first one next to the chasm, I did not manage to make those two or three steps because I can't tell you exactly but I know that had I made that, either second or third, I would have dropped down so that I stopped at the very edge, and then we were ordered to go down on our knees. I did not manage to kneel, as I did, because the man behind me, as we were standing in this line, he simply pushed me into that chasm and that is when we once again heard the gunfire from behind our backs.
