utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you walked to the edge of that cliff and squatted down, can you describe or do you recall now about that abyss? Can you give us any estimate of the depth of the drop?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: All I can say is the place where I was, it didn't look like that, because I was somewhere in the back of the column. The place where I was, it was a little bit like this, but the column was to the right of me and it was perhaps 20 or 30 metres long, the men were lined up, so the place where we were, the chasm was so steep, this is what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've indicated for your hand I'm going to describe it for the record, that the witness indicated an almost 90 degree angle as far as the edge of the cliff. I think he actually indicated that the cliff slightly protruded over the abyss. Would you agree, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, Mr. Koumjian, do you have any photographs of this area or videos of this place?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. We have photographs. We will have them at the next break. Obviously taken much later but yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said you were at one end of the line and -- am I correct from what I understood you to say, at the point you were at, it was a little less steep, the cliff, there was a little angle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the man behind you pushed you. Is it correct that the two lines were right next to each other at the edge of the cliff?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I am repeating it once more. I didn't manage to make two or three paces. I can't remember. But had I made three paces I would have already fallen down the cliff so I was already pushed, but we didn't even manage to kneel and by that time, by the time we knelt, they had -- kneeled down they had already fired into our backs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That was my question. When did you hear the gunfire in relation to when you were pushed? Was it before or after you were pushed?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: You could hear it immediately, as we were kneeling down. At that time, I wasn't pushed yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you recall about your fall?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It was like this: I remember, because I remained conscious throughout, I didn't lose consciousness, I turned over my head and then I rolled down the rocks and then I was stopped by rocks and by some growth that was quite low to the ground, but other people further up had been shot and I could see a man with half his head missing, who rolled over my body and continued to roll down. So when I stopped, there were already a lot of people at the bottom who had been shot at and who had fallen down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any estimate of the number of metres that you fell?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It was all very fast. I don't know exactly how many metres it was. I can't say. And I haven't been back there yet, although I do want to go back but I haven't been back to that place yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you reached the bottom, did you smell anything?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I could smell something bad. During my fall, I could see clothing around, so I believe that we were not the only group that was harmed in that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you smelled something bad, I don't know if you had ever smelled a decaying human body, but were you familiar with that smell?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you smelled that at the bottom, did you feel -- did you think that that was the odour of human decay, a human body decaying?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you hear the shooting go on for?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: The shooting went on for so long, for as long as -- for the time that it took me to get up from where I was and cross to the other side of the water. During my fall, there was water down at the bottom, water flowing, so I got up and the impetus to get up was given to me by my colleague who was there before me who got up and left. Then I also got up and started moving after him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't believe there is a problem. We'll use his first name. Was that Bahrija that you saw?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so you know, he's given us permission to use his name, just so you don't feel concerned about that.

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him, what did the two of you do? You and Bahrija?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: He gave me the impetus to get up and to follow him. Then we crossed to the other side of that river and we passed between two water mills that were there on the river. They were made of wood. And we crossed to the other side. The other side was covered by a wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to select a couple of photographs and show them to Mr. Ackerman first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Garibovic, do you know what happened to the people on the other bus that you saw when you got off your bus?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I was under such stress after that that I simply was not able to move from there. Bahrija left me for a moment and went towards the cliff, from the other side, and he saw how they were bringing, from the first bus that was standing in front of our bus, certain numbers of people and they were killing them. And those people also ended up down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the people from what you call the first bus, the bus that was in front of yours, were taken off after you and killed in smaller groups, according to what Bahrija told you; is that correct? Bahrija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the usher just bring these to Mr. Ackerman? I'll get to them later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you and Bahrija do?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Bahrija looked as if he were in a much better state than I was. He was not so beaten up and he was psychologically in better shape than I was. We waited until morning in that place. I say morning but maybe it was about 3.00 or 4.00 a.m. Then we started to climb, to go up through the forest, because the terrain was steep. But I didn't say this. After the shooting stopped, you could still hear the sounds of people who had not died yet. You could hear them. They were giving signs of life. They were moaning. I cannot claim exactly whether they were people from our group who had survived and who were going somewhere, who were climbing up or maybe they were people who were hit and who were down at the bottom in that group just lying there but were still giving signs of life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you hear them moaning? Throughout the time that you were staying at the bottom waiting for daylight?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It went on the entire time that we were there, and we were there until perhaps about 3.00 a.m. That whole evening and until 3.00 a.m. The people could be heard for several hours and then after that, there was silence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated you've never been back to that spot, and I don't know, has anyone ever shown you photographs of an area that they believe was spot of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody ever showed me photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know if this would assist. The photographs that I was shown are attached to a Rule 92 bis witness proffer that I have agreed to and you're going to get that testimony and all the photographs, more than what he has there, and if it's awkward for this witness to try to identify them or something, you're going to have them in any event anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's show them to the witness. Perhaps we will have some sort of an indication from him whether the terrain is familiar or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before I do that, Your Honour, I have the witness's testimony from the Omarska case. May that be marked as Exhibit P1538?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Chuqing just check the sequence and -- the number sequence, make sure that it is 1538. I usually rely 100 per cent on Ms. Gustin. Is that correct? Yes. So that will be P1538. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't looked at this with a view toward whether there should be redactions or not. I think there are none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine that there aren't any, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think they are not. I hadn't considered this might be offered as an exhibit so I hadn't looked through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I went through it more or less the details of what we have now. It's a little bit basically about the Vlasic itself. It's exactly almost a replica of what he's testified now. And much of what he's testified today he was not asked upon in the other case. So I don't -- and there was no mention of your client. Yes. The only thing that there is that he was eventually treated for wounds in Banja Luka but again, in the Banja Luka hospital and there are some -- yes, some, but he didn't testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll go over that in I think more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I read it yesterday so I know pretty much what it says. All I was saying to you was that it hadn't occurred to me that the Prosecution might offer it as an exhibit so I hadn't read it from the standpoint of whether I would agree to its submission or not or contest its admission. If that's the case that they want to offer it as an exhibit it seems to me we are kind of in a position we are with the rest of these witnesses where we are offering their prior testimony that that pretty much forms the direct examination and we could avoid going through a lot of this stuff over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was my suggestion in the first place to Mr. Koumjian at the beginning of the session, the sitting today. But any way --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's not what -- we hadn't anticipated using it at all but Mr. Ackerman brought up the offer to stipulate to the names included in that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was being proposed as under Rule 92 bis, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No. This witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. Let me check to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is another witness whose testimony is virtually identical, Your Honour, that I have agreed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, it was viva voce. But anyway if we can speed up, accelerate as much as we could, that would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I have five photographs marked P1539, 1 through 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes and usher, please, put them one by one on the ELMO and the witness can follow either directly on the ELMO or on his screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Garibovic you may either look at the screen or look at the photograph to your right but that photograph that's on the screen, do you recognise that spot?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I've said many times where I was, and the place where we stopped was at a bend in the road. So according to what I remember, and to what I said, this could be this bend here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the next photograph we understand you can only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's for the record, does the first photo that has been shown have a marking on it or an ERN number or something? Can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have marked it with the exhibit number attachment 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even if it's going to be exhibited later on but at least we will have a reference indicated now because otherwise we will lose complete track of which photo he's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Not an ERN number but that was P1539-1 and this would be P1539-2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this appears to be a photograph of an abyss, a cliff. Does this appear to be consistent to you with what you remember the cliff looking like that you fell down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't -- Mr. Garibovic, don't be afraid if you -- because this is like any other cliffs. There are many cliffs like that near the village where I live. So if the Prosecutor asked me to say whether that is a cliff near where I live, I would say, looks like it. So don't worry, it's not that important. It's not going to change any -- anything if you say, "I don't know. I don't recognise that cliff or it looks like it, I mean they were falling down, they had time to look at the configuration of the cliff, in any case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can state the following. On our right side, if you go in this direction, it's true that this road was like that, and that there were rocks on the right side. On the left side where we were was the abyss and the river was flowing down at the bottom. In that period, in August, there was water flowing down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, now we are looking at photograph number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again just any brief comment that you may have on this photograph, Mr. Garibovic.

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now you can see. We are going downhill. That's shown on this photograph. And I remember that. There was an incline, if this is an incline here, and it seems to me that this photograph does show an incline. This part of the road here. If this is an incline or if the road goes down here, then I remember that we were going down the road like this. And it's true that this could -- this road could be going downwards like I say. That's what is shown here on this photograph, a descent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think the photograph needs to be...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, I think so. I'm trying to make heads or tails of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any comment about this photograph, Mr. Garibovic? None is necessary.

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this part here is where the river flows and that this part here is the end of the abyss, but it seems that at the time when this photograph was taken, there was no water there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This seems to be taken from the top, no? From an elevated position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you repeat what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: He said he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't know, okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph, please. Is that it? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I have those photographs?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Garibovic, can you tell the Judges what happened after 3.00 a.m. when you and Bahrija climbed up -- what happened over the next few days?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly whether it was two or three days that we were wandering on Mount Vlasic. Bahrija looked much better than I did. He was in much better psychological shape, and he wasn't so bruised from the fall, not as bruised as I was. I had had a much harder time. I had heavy bruising all over my body. In the morning I was all swollen up. So that for the entire road that we were going, he was helping me when we were climbing up the hills and going through the woods, when the going was rough, he would help me. We didn't dare give any signs of ourselves or go and talk to anybody. We did pass by houses but we couldn't call at them. We couldn't call at those houses. We did the best we could with food. We drank water in one place we found wild strawberries so that's what we ate. First we were wandering around and there was no water but then after a while we found some water and we drank there. However, later we had stomach problems and that was it. Mostly, we spent three days wandering around Mount Vlasic. We didn't dare make ourselves known to everyone. After a heavy rain one day, towards evening, we had gotten soaked through. This is a forest area, and the rains there are very strong and cold. So after a while we saw this shepherd who was looking after sheep and we decided to ask for help. We went up to him and asked him if he could help us. He gave us a little bit of cheese and bread. And he said that he couldn't help us any more than that. However, after this help that he gave us, in the meantime he went, he knew the terrain well, and he reported -- this place where he went where soldiers were, was called Galica. It was a settlement. And there was a kind of military post there. There were some mountain houses there. But the army was stationed there. So he went there and he reported us. However, because we arrived at that place where we were captured first, and when we got there, the soldier who was at that line stopped us and we -- when we went up to him, he said the following, "Is anyone else coming?" And we said no. And he said, "If anyone else appears, I will kill you right away." But nobody else appeared, nothing happened, so then he -- so that he wouldn't leave that line where he was, he took his rifle and fired into the air so that somebody would come from those rooms where the soldiers were stationed, and which were nearby. After the shot, one soldier came and he took us towards those little houses. When we came up to the houses, a soldier came out, another one, other than the one who brought us there, and he ordered us to lie down on the ground and to turn our heads down towards the grass. Then one of them said, "Go and bring a knife so that we can slaughter them." Then a couple of minutes later, there was a command issued for us to stand up. Then a soldier took us and brought us inside a room which was full of soldiers, and there were beds there lined up in that room. One of them already said that he knew Bahrija from somewhere when we went inside, he asked us if we had any money, if we had any papers. I had 50 German marks. That was confiscated. One of them took that right away and already figured out how much alcohol he could buy for that amount of money. After that, it was decided that they should drive us, but we didn't know where. We were put into a truck, together with two soldiers who were sitting in the back, and we were taken to some command or other. I don't know where this command actually was. I can say that they treated us fairly when we got there. Since I wasn't wearing anything, I wandered three days on -- over Vlasic with no clothes. I only had one pair of torn pants that I was wearing. I had a torn shirt which had gotten soaked in the rain so I was holding that in my hand when we got there, they gave us something to wear and they gave us something to eat for dinner. They didn't ask us anything, where we were from, who we were, nobody asked us anything. I also wish to state the following: That place when we came, the first -- at first when we were captured, they asked us where we were from and we said we were from the convoy, this was the first place that we came to. But they didn't ask anything about the convoy, what it was or anything like that. So they took us and drove us in this truck for a while. We got to the command. They gave us dinner to eat. They gave us clothes to wear. We put their military uniform on. That's what they had and that's what we put on, the military shirts and so on. After that, we were taken in a luxury vehicle, I don't know what model car it was, we were taken to Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you interviewed in Skender Vakuf about the massacre on Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Like this: When Bahrija and I arrived there, there were already some who had succumbed earlier and who had asked for help and who had been brought there earlier. Should I give you the names of those people who were already there before us or perhaps that is not important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think if the names are necessary, we can do it in private session but these are other survivors of the massacre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you require the names, Mr. Ackerman? Okay. We can do without. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were other survivors of the massacre, correct? You were interviewed by military about the massacre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then is it true that at a later point you were also interviewed by police officer -- a police investigator and a judge? Is that correct? In Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just add one other thing. That evening, I mean we arrived there in the evening, that is where we spent the night and in the morning we were all taken for examination. We had to undergo three different interrogations here in Skender Vakuf. The first one was, I don't know whether he was a colonel or a major or something but he was a rather high-ranking officer and when I was interrogated he said to me, the following: "Garibovic, what you are going to tell me, see that you tell us just as it was, to speak the truth. And in future, if anyone asks you anything about it, just try to do the same." And after what I told him, he read out the statement to me and I signed it. And supposedly everybody did this. But then we were taken to the police once again and made identical statements there and then we went to the crime investigation department. So that was what was in Skender Vakuf. We had to give our statements three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we are on the subject of your statements, you also were interviewed by a judge along with I believe four other survivors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It is. That was after we left the hospital. The CID of the Banja Luka Public Security Service took us to the Court and there we again had to give statements. But let me put it this way: The gentleman who questioned us never stopped, because he'd get interested in something or all he said was, "Go on, go on, go on, go on. Finished? Sign. The next one."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the interviews of all five of you take with the judge?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Not very long. I can't tell you exactly, but perhaps half an hour, as far as I'm concerned. I remember well how it was all typed out and that I signed it in the end, and we all went through the same procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The five -- the question was for the five of you, how long did the interviewing process last? Not just yours. The five of you altogether, was it just 30 minutes as you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It could have taken two and a half, three hours perhaps, for the five of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I was right in my mind. Yes, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Skender Vakuf were you taken to a hospital in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which hospital were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: First we were taken to a hospital which was in the centre. That was the surgery department. But there we stayed only perhaps one day or so. And the next day we were taken to Paprikovac that was a hospital out of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that a -- was that an eye hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Where we were hospitalised at Paprikovac. It was on the fourth floor, and yes, that was the eye hospital or the eye department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Judges the treatment and the conditions you lived in in those hospitals in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: We were beaten. They wouldn't leave us alone for a single moment, for those 21 days. We were beaten all the time. We were beaten by the staff, by the personnel, by those who came from the outside. The guards beat us. They would go on all night long, forcing us to learn these Serb songs, and they did all the worst, and that's all there is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to drink water, all you wanted?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Like this, for 20 days, we were forbidden, we were not allowed to get off the bed without asking for permission. Prior to our asking for whatever, we had to raise like this, three fingers. This room was glass-walled and the guard who was watching us, he walked all the time so when he would see the sign he would pretend he didn't, and at times you had to keep our fingers for half an hour up to ask for help. But he would never come into ask what was the matter. And if he did pay attention, that -- he would come in and beat you. And that is how it went on. We spent a lot of time there and we were never allowed to ask for anything or anything. And at times they would force us to keep our faces down in the pillows for two or more hours and it was hot but you had to turn your head face down to the pillow and try to breathe like that. They beat us with cables, with sticks, with whatever. They simply wouldn't leave us alone after all the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in your room who were survivors of the Vlasic Mountain massacre?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other individuals in the room who were not from the massacre, who were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember well a man who was called Milan Rozankovic, he was brought because he'd allegedly been captured somewhere in the Dubocac. And when he arrived, all he had was a bottle with him and he was bleeding into it. He was beaten there in the hospital so that they had to put that bottle on the other side. They beat him and they would beat him until he would lose consciousness, and I learned from the colleague who was the last one to leave, that Rozankovic succumbed to the beatings. He was beaten the most of all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- we didn't hear what he said in and the transcript reflects that we didn't hear what he said where this person was captured. He said he had been captured somewhere in the...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard somewhere in the bottom but again I agree with you that it doesn't show in the transcript but there is the arrow which means they will fill it up later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd kind of like to know what is because I might want to question him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, you said, "I remember well a man who was called Milan Rozankovic. He was brought because he had allegedly been captured somewhere in." Where was he captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dubocac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that an area -- do you know where that is?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it anywhere near where you were captured?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. This was the first time I heard of the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the doctors treat you and what knowledge did they have of the mistreatment that others were -- the beatings that were going on?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Like this: Those shifts there, the guards, and I think they took shifts, two or three times a day, they ordered us as follows. When the doctor came or comes on his round, when the doctor asks you how are you, you must say that you are all right. You may not ask for any medicines. You may not talk about anything. How are you, how are you doing today? Fine. So that when a doctor would come and ask us how we were, we were say that we were fine, and so he would do his round, dress the wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how a particular doctor treated and greeted Mr. Rozankovic, the Croat gentleman you said was beaten to death in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was Dr. Stanisic. He was -- he showed the most repulsion towards us of all the doctors. When he would come in he would say, "Ah, Rozankovic does it hurt? It hurts, doesn't it? See how it hurts? That's how our people hurt." So he would move from one to the other one of us but he would always stop by Rozankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Garibovic, you spent a couple months, three months, in the Trnopolje camp approximately. How do you compare the time in the hospital in Banja Luka to your time in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that I fared worse in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Garibovic, do you know when the people in the Trnopolje camp learned about the massacre on Mount Vlasic of the convoy that had left the camp on the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That same evening, I think, because women and children had gone through. They said that very many men had been separated and they could not say what had happened, except that they'd been separated. And then -- well, one could find out what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe confusing to us. You said the women said that they had been separated. Was it your understanding that women arrived in Travnik and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you for a moment. I hate to do this, Mr. Koumjian in the middle of a question but it's becoming a little bit confusing. Your previous question was, "Mr. Garibovic, do you know when the people in the Trnopolje camp learned about the massacre on Mount Vlasic of the convoy that had left the camp on the 21st of August." I suppose anyone who left Trnopolje on the 21st of August never turned back to Trnopolje camp, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to explain. Let me try to explain it. I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, go -- I mean, I will allow you to ask whatever question you like but please, put it in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was going to object because I don't know unless there is some foundation for knowledge that he would have about what people in Trnopolje camp learned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think he didn't mean the people in Trnopolje because it doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I do mean that I'm sorry but I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless you have some other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My fault, I'll try to explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Garibovic, did your brother Ahmet did he try to get on the convoy on the 21st and was unable to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you left the Trnopolje camp in August, do you know if the people in the camp had access to Sarajevo Radio? Were people able to hear Sarajevo Radio from the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I believe one could hear it. Of course people who had radios or transistors, because there were frequent power cuts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother Ahmet, he survived the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you speak to him about what he learned about the convoy that you had been on? Did he tell you what the word was in Trnopolje, what people had heard about the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Like this: The next day, Mr. Kuruzovic came to them and said, "Listen, there has been some gunfire on Vlasic but it was something, nothing, nothing much happened, and a new convoy would be put together shortly."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if before Mr. Kuruzovic spoke to the inmates in Trnopolje, people had heard on the radio about the massacre? Or that people were missing that did not arrive in Travnik with the rest of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said it. It was right that evening that one learned that men had been separated in that convoy -- from that convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to that, because I think it's a matter of importance, when you were in Trnopolje camp, did you ever hear anything about a massacre at the Keraterm camp? Was that widely known?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did hear about it when that happened, and later on, too, from my brother, because he was in Keraterm throughout and also from other people who came, that it also, that one night a horrible massacre happened there too one night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that widely known among the people at Trnopolje, that this massacre had occurred?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Judges how you eventually were released from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: As somebody who had recovered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were you visited by the -- were you taken in by Merhamet in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said something about it. After I was released from the hospital, the criminal investigation department of the public security centre in Banja Luka took us over and I already said that we made those statements. And then they asked us if we had any relations in Banja Luka, and some did, some didn't, but they couldn't find any of them when they checked so that gentleman who drove us said, "Well, if Merhamet didn't take you over, I don't know what to do with you." But then when he went to Merhamet and made some inquiries there then those people took us in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While were you being housed by Merhamet, were you registered by the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: You see, I forgot to mention that, the International Red Cross registered us while we were at Stokica [phoen], still that is in the hospital there. However, the guard who guarded us, he immediately collected all those cards and took them away and we never saw them until we were released from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were -- how did you get out of the area of Banja Luka, out of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: How? We left with the help of those internationals. They came to Merhamet. I mean UNPROFOR, they came there, they put us in their vehicles, then took us to Trnopolje, and on the way there, they said, "Well, if you need some water or to relieve yourselves, they had provided everything there so that we had not to go out and they went to Mr. Kuruzovic in the Red Cross, they arranged with all the papers, they signed whatever we -- we needed to sign to leave Republika Srpska, and said that we were renouncing our property and all the rest, so we did not get off the vehicles in Trnopolje and that was that. We arrived in Trnopolje, these papers were already done by that time, and together with other inmates, we reached Karlovac and from Karlovac, then Switzerland, Germany and that was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I gather your brother Ahmet was aware that you were on the convoy on the 21st of August. Do you know when your family became aware that you had survived?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It was after I left the hospital, because I called them from Merhamet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you rejoin your wife?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: In Germany, in January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Garibovic, do you know anyone who was on those two buses on Vlasic Mountain and did not survive?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name those individuals that you can recall right now, that you knew?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Like this: There are eight neighbours of mine who were all called Garibovic, Kemal, then the father and son, also Kadir and his son Elvir Kararic, they also lived in my village but they had a different last name. So Kemal Garibovic, Vasif Garibovic, Tajib Garibovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone who you knew from your work in the factory?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the manager of the factory in Kozarac, Mala Privreda?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Whilst I still worked for Mala Privreda, it was Asim Fazlic. He was my ex-manager and his brother, and they were with me in this column that I mentioned. They were recognisable by the clothes they were wearing because they had a kind of sweat-suits which were rather bright coloured so that they were pretty conspicuous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Jasim Fazlic and his brother are missing to this day, to your knowledge, along with all the Garibovics and people from your village that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, have their remains ever been located? Have their bodies ever been found?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, never. Nobody was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garibovic, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Koumjian. Mr. Ackerman, is there a problem with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Garibovic, you are going to be cross-examined now by Mr. Ackerman who is the lead counsel for the accused Mr. Brdjanin. Mr. Ackerman you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can still say good morning, Mr. Garibovic, for another four minutes. How are you? First thing I should tell you is that all of us here on I think I speak probably for everybody in the courtroom, we are -- we have a lot of sympathy for what happened to you on that day, we are sorry that it happened and I hope you understand that. I'm going to be very brief with you. I have very few questions to ask you and we will get through this very quickly if you can listen carefully and answer my questions with as short an answer as you possibly can. Would you try to do that?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk to you first about Trnopolje. And some of the things I'm going to ask you are kind of a repetition of what you've already said today. When you first went to Trnopolje, you in fact saw your wife and children there but what you said in your statement was the next day, you couldn't find her but then later she came to visit you, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when she came to visit you after you couldn't find her any more, you learned that the authorities at Trnopolje were letting women and children who had relatives or friends living in the area leave Trnopolje and go live with them, right?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she was able to go to Sivci?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout the period when she was still in the area, she was allowed to come and visit you at Trnopolje, bring you food, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said in that -- in your statement that before she left on that convoy on the train, apparently, the railroad, that she was not required to sign any kind of papers.

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She was not, was she?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Trnopolje, you knew that the commander was a person named Slobodan Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a military person, was he?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his office was in a bar across from the outpatient clinic, a bar that was called Lovac?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was his office when you first got to Trnopolje and it was still his office in early August, was it not, when you went to see him?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice that he had a fairly serious drinking problem? Were you aware of that, that he drank a lot of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how I would be able to notice that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, perhaps you could move the microphones nearer to the witness or ask the witness to move nearer to the microphones. Or do both. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a point, was there not, when you went to see him in his office to try to get permission to leave?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, there is I think a document for me to sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice that he had a drinking problem, that he was drinking on that day?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You've told us that during your stay you didn't see anyone killed or see anyone getting beaten, and it's also true, isn't it, that you were not beaten during any of the time you stayed in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I personally was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the guards were? Do you know what organisation they were from? Were they military? What were they?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: The guards that were there came from Prijedor every day, by bus from Prijedor to Trnopolje. They wore military uniforms, of course, and they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's the case, isn't it, that there was no fence completely surrounding Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: The fence was put up and dismantled as it suited whoever was there. It was put up and then taken down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But never was there a fence surrounding the entire complex, was there?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It was too large to be completely encircled by a fence, but small fences were put up and people were placed inside. For example, when the people from Omarska came, they were detained separately, a small encirclement was made and then when the men from Keraterm came, they were also enclosed. However, when the International Red Cross was supposed to visit the camp, this was all taken down and people were mixed up. On whose orders this was done, I really wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were there almost three months, and that period of time you're talking about right now was right close to the end, after the journalists came but prior to that, don't you know that people were able to go in and out of Trnopolje at night, pretty much at will?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this did not happen at night. Nobody went in or went out of the Trnopolje camp, and I can tell you that for a fact. I was there for three months. There was shooting sometimes all night, at Trnopolje, and I don't know why people would leave Trnopolje and where they would go, and for what reason. Nobody came into or left Trnopolje at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So anybody who would say that they did that would not be telling the truth, I take it?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. During the day, I'm not saying people did go around to Sivci and so on during the day. However, at night, nobody dared to leave Trnopolje, to walk around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that the people that were at Trnopolje were being protected by guards or by local Serb people from extremists on the outside who would come in at night and do bad things?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many convoys of people would you say left Trnopolje before the 10th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Does Mr. Ackerman mean to say the 10th of August or does he mean the 21st the day he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Garibovic, the date that you have to pay attention for is the 10th of August of 1992. And you are being asked if you know how many convoys of people you would say left Trnopolje before that particular date. 10th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was like this: I can say, but I cannot say that with certainty, that there were several rail convoys, and those were the closed-type carriages and one of them was the one that my wife left with. Then there were other convoys that were organised, but all the convoys that were organised would go via Trnopolje and onwards. There were also convoys with buses and trucks, and there were also four or five of those. I was at Trnopolje so I know, but I cannot say whether there were two or three, how many, but in any case, all the convoys went through Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't very precise in my question. Let me try to do a better job. I'm only interested in convoys in which people who were at Trnopolje left in. I know that you saw lots of convoys that went -- that were taking people from other places but people from Trnopolje, how many convoys do you think there were before the 10th of August that actually took people out of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand you again but let me try to answer your question. All men from --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you ought to give me a chance to be clear?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went into Trnopolje in May, sometime near the end of May, and you left on the 21st of August. You know that there were some internationals who showed up there early in August, around the 10th. There were journalists who came there and some other people. And what I want to know is between the time that you went in there and the time that these internationals came, how many convoys transported people out of Trnopolje to other places? And I don't ask you to be precise because I know you can't so I'm not looking for a precise number.

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I think when the International Red Cross came to Trnopolje for the first time, so I don't know from that time whether there was any convoy. I can't tell you. I really don't know how many convoys there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were convoys prior to the 10th of August?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people left Trnopolje on those convoys prior to the 10th of August? Just -- and I know you can't be precise. What would be your estimate?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It's hard to say. I am repeating once more, all the places that had been cleansed in the Prijedor municipality and the surrounding places, all the people from that area were mostly brought to Trnopolje, and the next day they would leave. So some people would then get mixed up. Some people that had already been in Trnopolje would leave as well as those who had just arrived. So I cannot really answer precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I think you've done the best you can, and I appreciate it. Now, there came a time on the 21st of August, when you actually yourself got on a bus and left Trnopolje. And the first time that bus you were on stopped was at the Kozarac junction, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there, you say that you were joined -- that that convoy was joined by some big trucks with trailers. Do you know how many big trucks with trailers joined the convoy at that point?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, because I couldn't see how long the column was because I was in the bus. We waited for the column to form. I can't say how many trucks there were or other vehicles for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once those trucks got there, because your buses were rather crowded, you were invited, weren't you, to leave the bus and go, get on one of those trucks where it might not be so crowded?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A certain number of people left the buses and crossed into the -- moved into the trucks, which were not as overcrowded as the buses. However, I did not leave the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I want to establish is that had you wanted to, you could have, apparently, you were invited to?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The convoy then proceeded, I think you said, to Skender Vakuf and then after you left there, the convoy stopped several times and you said that you saw during those stops you saw soldiers passing by and looking into the buses? Correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had not seen these soldiers before that period of time when you left Skender Vakuf, had you?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was also at that time that for the first time you saw this man with the red beret and the walkie-talkie, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was the convoy completely intact still at that point? Were the trucks and the trailers and all the buses still part of that convoy? Was it this same convoy that had left the Kozarac junction?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we get to that point where you were asked -- you and several others were asked to get off the bus you were on and get on a different bus, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you said in your testimony -- your previous testimony, at page 5828, was that after you boarded those buses, the whole convoy was allowed to pass and proceed, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get any sense of how many vehicles passed and proceeded the bus you were then on?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many vehicles, but in any case, the vehicles passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to that convoy that was allowed to pass on and proceed?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: The convoy reached Turbe, because these were the people from the convoy that remained behind, women, children, the elderly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That convoy that went on after you had changed buses, to your knowledge actually made it to a safe area, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you don't know of anything that would have kept the soldiers that were there at that spot from simply taking everybody off that convoy and killing all of them that day, do you? They could have done that, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to go to that period of time after you had been walking through the woods for I think you said about three days. You eventually wound up in the hands of some Serb soldiers again, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they took you to Skender Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... survivors?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were fed and were you given clothes?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you made statements to police and the military and the criminal investigation division?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were told by this high-ranking officer that you should tell the truth and you did tell the truth, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that I told the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told them that you were with a group that had been lined up along the edge of that -- of that cliff and basically had been massacred, that a few of you had survived but that most everyone else was killed?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point in time, these Serb soldiers and these Serb police knew that you were a survivor of that massacre that you had witnessed that massacre and that you had described this man with a red beret and a Motorola, walkie-talkie, as being the one who appeared to be in charge?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after providing them with that knowledge, do you know that if the other survivors basically told the truth too about what they had experienced?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I think that they also told the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall one of the survivors that was with you being a young man with a broken ankle, who couldn't walk?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next thing that happened was they took you all to the hospital in Banja Luka, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This same young man with the broken ankle, do you remember seeing him as a survivor of this massacre in either of the hospitals you were in in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: May I say this, sir? We were placed in three rooms. We could not go to the other rooms, and I repeat this once again, we were not permitted to get up and out of our bed. I don't know who was in the other rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand all that. My question wasn't an accusation. I just want to know if you ever saw this person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Mr. Ackerman, he has already -- he had already answered to a previous question of yours, asking him whether -- do -- your question was, "Do you recall one of the survivors that was with you being a young man with a broken ankle who couldn't walk?" And his answer was no. So how could he answer you in any way to your second question whether this young man with the broken ankle, do you remember seeing him as a survivor of this massacre in either of the hospitals in Banja Luka. He doesn't seem to know of anyone with a broken ankle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. I think I've gotten there. My first question, Your Honour was about when he was at Skender Vakuf with the other survivors and then I wondered if he might have seen this person this person in the hospital in Banja Luka, and I got my answer he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you surrendered or were captured by these soldiers before you were taken to Skender Vakuf, they could have just shot you there, of course, I assume, couldn't they, if they had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It's true what you say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once they took you to Skender Vakuf, and you made it clear that you were witnesses to what had happened there, they also could have shot you there, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon your release from the hospital in Banja Luka, you said you were taken before a Judge and again made a statement about what you had observed and experienced regarding this matter. I want to ask you just one question about that. Was that a civilian judge or was that judge wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It was a civilian judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you've already told us that all of the survivors that you were with at least went there and made a statement of their own experiences, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout the period that you had anything to do with the police there in Banja Luka, you were treated correctly and properly, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't have any contact with the police, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it the police that took you from the hospital to the judge?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: It was the criminal investigations service that took us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was that part of the police or part of the military?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: They were dressed in civilian clothes. I don't know what they were, but they wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They treated you correctly, didn't they, and properly?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They are the same people who took you to Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Merhamet is a Muslim charitable organisation that was operating in Banja Luka in August of 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct what you say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now have just a very few questions regarding your testimony today. You were asked about when you boarded the bus at Trnopolje, if Slobodan Kuruzovic was there, and if young men were allowed to board the buses for the first time, and you indicated that that was the case, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was standing next to the bus and everyone was boarding the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever know that an English man by the name of Paddy Ashdown visited Trnopolje in early August? Were you ever aware of that, a politician from England?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did know that there had been journalists there?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that, because they did come to Trnopolje on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you learned since these events that serious efforts were made to relieve the situation at Trnopolje and get the people there moved out, exchanged, taken to other countries or something?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No one in Trnopolje knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm -- what I'm saying is do you know that now? Did you learn that afterwards?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't learn that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It's the case, isn't it, that after your convoy left Skender Vakuf, you no longer saw any of the people from any of those original people that were escorting you when you left Trnopolje? All of a sudden, it was all these soldiers and the man with the red beret, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that while you were in Trnopolje, people were brought there from Omarska and I don't have your exact words but you said they were all hairy, they had beards, they were very dirty. Am I correct that that's your position?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I said that about the men who came from Keraterm and that is also -- it also applies to those who came from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that the people in Omarska had been filmed by international journalists just a few days before that? And have you ever seen that film?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I've seen the film but I don't know when it was filmed or when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in the film, you didn't see people that were dirty and bearded and in the condition you described on their arrival at Omarska, did you?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They were hidden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there but I saw the people who came from Omarska. I saw what they looked like. I saw the state they were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know that journalists also came to Keraterm and photographed the people that had come there from Omarska? Did you ever see those films?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: First it assumes facts not in evidence. And in fact I think that's not correct. No journalist that I know of went to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer the question because then you are answering the question but in any case I am accepting your objection. There is no evidence that he was in Keraterm in any case. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just misspoke, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I intended to ask was, do you know journalists also came to Trnopolje and photographed the people that had come there from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that and that is true. And they were taping people from Keraterm who had arrived, and this footage travelled the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were registered by the ICRC in Banja Luka, in the hospital, you recall that happening?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: That was done perhaps some ten days later, at Paprikovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were able to speak with the ICRC in private?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not able to speak with them in private?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, sir, because men who were guarding us were there with them. They had weapons with them and they were there all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell the ICRC about the way that were you being treated?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't dare do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you know that not being allowed to speak to you in private was against ICRC policy and they would not have done that unless they could have seen you privately? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, whether he knows ICRC policy or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long will it take you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ten minutes will require us because we have been sitting for an hour and a half so the option is we either go on for another ten minutes and then it will be over or we break for half an hour and then resume. We go on? We go -- the technicians as well? I can't see behind. Okay, Mr. Koumjian you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now the pressure is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to keep it as concise as possible, please. Re-examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir I just want to ask you a few questions concerning what the Defence attorney asked you about the investigation of the crime and the interviews you had with the police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need a couple of minutes to change the tape so in the meantime you can think about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's the first election I've ever won.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That means you can go ahead. Yes, Mr. Koumjian, I suggest to you repeat the question or I can read it out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll repeat it I'll try to shorten it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in 1992, when you spoke to the police and the judge in Banja Luka, did anyone ever show you any photographs or have you attend any identification procedures, any kind of identification parade or line up to see if you could recognise the perpetrators of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't shown anything. I wasn't mentioned anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone show you photographs of the police who were on duty to escort that convoy that day?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have recognised in 1992 the man in the red beret that you saw giving the orders and saying, "This is where we do the exchange, the living for the living and the dead, it is known" if you had seen him in 1992 would you have recognised him?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the hospital did you speak to one of the survivors who told you that he recognised one of the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember one of the survivors telling you the name of one of the people that he recognised the police at the massacre?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: A mention -- a name came up, yes, yes, a name was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what name was that?

utterances.speaker: EMSUD GARIBOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Mrdja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Garibovic, that brings to an end your testimony in this trial. And very soon you will be escorted out of this courtroom by the usher who will, together with other officers of the court, look after you and attend to your needs to enable you to return to your family. Before you leave this courtroom, it is my duty as the Presiding Judge, in my name and also in the name of the other two Judges, as well as that of the Tribunal in general to thank you for having accepted to come and give evidence. I thank you once more and you will now be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wish to thank you, Mr. Koumjian and you Mr. Ackerman for being so cooperative today, as usual and enabling us to finish even earlier than scheduled and to enable this gentleman to return to his family and not spend the weekend here. Thank you, we'll meet on Tuesday morning. Mr. Usher, please escort the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally there will be a decision, I signed it this morning, a decision being handed down on the motion by General Talic in this case. So please have a look at it. All right? Anything else? Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a Rule 92 bis report. I have finished, Your Honour. There are two of the witnesses who I have made inquiry of Ms. Korner about. I can't file my final response to you until I get an answer from her. I hope to have that as soon as I get it I can file it rather immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 94 I'll start working on this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So until Tuesday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 12.35 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of December, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
